## Making a Website with Quarto and Github Pages {#sec-make-website}

Having a [professional website](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02310-6) is increasingly important for researchers and scientists. It serves as a central location for your publications, projects, and professional information. When colleagues, potential collaborators, or employers search for you online, your website provides a controlled first impression. This tutorial will guide you through creating and hosting your own website using Quarto and GitHub Pages.

### Hosting
To have a website viewable by the world it must be hosted on a server that is viewable by the world. For example, it cannot be behind an institutional firewall (as are most of the computers at the University of Waterloo). And if you host on a University or Company server you have the potential of being limited in what you can share, how often you can update, or you may be required to adhere to certain styles and formats mandated by the institution's brand. One way to avoid this is to find an external hosting site. A modest fee would allow you to have a virtual server in the cloud, but the example we will use here to get you started is a free service available to those with Github accounts: [Github Pages](https://pages.github.com/). 

### Testing Github Pages

:::callout-warning
Github and Quarto can change their procedures from time to time, and even minor changes in the file format can have big effects on whether things work or you get an error. Go slow. Read error messages. Your first assumption should be that you made a mistake, but if you are careful and verify that things are exactly as depicted here then you could consider if some process has changed. The error message will be your guide. If you do find that something is out of date please generate an issue (if not a pull request) so that I can fix it, and others do not have to share your pain. 

Also, you must be careful to distinguish what is running where. You will have a repository on github **and** on your laptop. Changes propagate between the two only when send them from one to the other. Changes are your laptop must be pushed to Github. Github changes must be pulled to your laptop. 

Make sure you know what the `localhost` means. Quarto can run a web server on your laptop and open the page in your browser. It will look like a web page from the internet, but it isn't. It is what the internet would see if you sent things to Github. If the address bar in your browser shows `localhost` you are running locally. If it shows <username>.github.io you are on the internet. 

:::

Assuming you have created your Github account you should be able to create a minimal webpage in a few steps. 

1. Go to your Github personal dashboard and create a new repository. The repo **must** be named your username.github.io. 
2. Use your terminal on your laptop to clone this repo to your local computer. 
   If you are using an ssh key for your authentication make sure you copy the ssh clone address and not the "https" one. 
3. On your laptop cd into the correct directory using a terminal (inside VS Code is fine, but I find it much more difficult to keep track of where I am when I do that). Using your *terminal* do `echo "hello world" > index.html.`
4. Verify that you can see that file in your directory. You can look with the `ls` command in your terminal.
5. Then `git add`, `git commit` , and `git push` that file to your Github remote. 
6. Open up your dashboard on github. Look at the repo. Refresh your browser, and verify you see `index.html` in the code window.
7. You should now have a website. To view it open up a *new* tab and type `<yourusername>.github.io` in the address bar. If you see anything other than "hello world" something went wrong. Figure that out now before proceeding or your life will get even more confusing. 


### Making a real website

    A "real" website will have many files in many folders. They will generally have an ending of `html`, at least for a basic, static, website. Writing html directly is tedious and we want to use our computer to avoid the tedium. Therefore we will use quarto so that we can write `qmd` files that are easier to write and understand, and where, if using VS Code, we can get lots of real time help and prompts. Then we will use the preview and render functions of quarto to convert our qmd files to html files. We will need to make sure that the location of the html files is distinct from our qmd for clarity. Thus, we will have to be careful in configuing both the files on our laptop that tell quarto what to do. And the repository on Github that tells Github what to do when it receives our pushed files. 
	
### Quarto Setup (you are doing this to the files on your laptop)

1. **Remove the test HTML file**:
   ```bash
   rm index.html
   ```

2. **Initialize a Quarto website project** in your repository folder (using the command in your terminal):
   ```bash
   quarto create project
   ```
   Choose "website" when prompted, and confirm overwriting the directory.

3. **Preview your site locally** to verify it's working:
   ```bash
   quarto preview
   ```
   Your browser should open displaying the default Quarto website.
   
   This will say `localhost` in your address bar. This is a local version. This is not a version that someone on the internet can see. 

4. **Customize the homepage** by editing the `index.qmd` file on your laptop. You can use VS Code. Replace the default content with your information:
   ```yaml
   ---
   title: "[Your Name]"
   ---
   
   ## About
   
   [Your academic position and affiliation]
   
   ## Research Interests
   
   [Your research areas and current projects]
   
   ## Contact
   
   [Your professional contact information]
   ```

5. **Configure for GitHub Pages deployment** by editing the `_quarto.yml` on your laptop. The key change here is the output_dir variable. We want to make sure that when quarto turns our qmd files into html that it stores those html files in a directory called "docs":
   ```yaml
   project:
     type: website
     output-dir: docs
   ```

6. **Build and deploy your site**. You are still doing this on your laptop.:
   ```bash
   quarto render  # <1> 
   git add . # <2>
   git commit -m "Initial Quarto website" # <3>
   git push # <4>
   ```
   
   1. This is where quarto reads our `_quarto.yml` file and all our `qmd` files and converts them to html and stores them in the docs directory.
   2. The dot here is a shortcut telling git to add everything new or changed.
   3. The `-m` means expect a message. Use short, but meaningful commit messages.
   4. This is the command that sends all our new and changed files to github. The default is `origin` for the remote name and `main` for the default branch. You can use other names, but then you have to list them explicitly. 

7. **Configure GitHub Pages** this you do through your browser on the Github page for your repository on Github; not your laptop: Navigate to your repository Settings → Pages → Source: Deploy from branch → Branch: main → Folder: /docs → Save

Your website should be available at <username>.github.io within a few minutes.

#### Customization Exercise

Practice modifying your website by completing these tasks:

- Create an About page by adding a new file called `about.qmd`
- Change the website theme by modifying the `theme` field in `_quarto.yml` (available themes include: cosmo, darkly, flatly, journal, litera, lumen, lux, materia, minty, morph, pulse, quartz, sandstone, simplex, sketchy, slate, solar, spacelab, superhero, united, vapor, yeti, zephyr)
- Add a navigation menu by updating the `navbar` section in `_quarto.yml`
- Include an image or figure on your homepage

Use `quarto preview` to test changes locally before committing and pushing to GitHub.

### Blog Project in Quarto

We just created a basic academic website with Quarto. In this variant you can make a blog as either a standalone website or something you can link to from the website you just created.  

The advantage of managing your blog in Quarto is that you get to take advantage of all the markdown language features. This is much more convenient than writing in html directly. You can also embed code and output just as you have been doing when you export your R code to html. 

### Creating a Blog with Quarto and GitHub Pages

While an academic website presents a polished professional identity, a blog serves a different purpose: regular, less formal expression of ideas, reflections on research, or documentation of learning. This tutorial builds on the website deployment skills you've already developed, but configures Quarto as a blog platform instead.

#### Why a Separate Blog Site?

Github limits you to one github pages website, but we don't want to overwrite the one you already made. The solution is to create a new "project" that also has a github-pages output, and then it will show up under your github name. That is why I can have a website at [brittAnderson.github.io](https://brittAnderson.github.io) and put these course notes as [brittanderson.github.io/uwlooP390](https://brittanderson.github.io/uwlooP390).

This separation also allows you to keep a clean, professional look for your public facing personal site, and also other sites that are more project specific or experimental. 

#### Creating the Blog Repository -- You do this on Github. 

Unlike your academic website which required the specific name `username.github.io`, a project site can have any repository name. We'll use `blog` for clarity.

1. **Create a new repository** on GitHub named `blog` (not `username.github.io`). Make it public.

:::callout-warning
Do **not** make the blog repository a subdirectory of your website repository. Having a git repository inside another git repository will cause great confusion for you, Github, git and me. 

:::

2. **Clone the repository** to your local machine:
   ```bash
   #pick the location where you want the respository to be
   cd <path>/somewhere-i-keep-my-repos/
   git clone https://github.com/username/blog.git
   cd blog
   ```
   

3. **Initialize a Quarto blog project**:
On your laptop, in either VS Code or terminal (which I find easier), cd to the directory that holds the "blog" repo you just created. Note that we will be using a specific keyword here to clue quarto into the correct template. We are making a *blog* not a *website*. At least as far as Quarto is concerned. We know that a blog is a website. 

   ```bash
   quarto create project
   ```
   Choose "blog" when prompted. If you are in the directory where the blog is to be located you can simply type a . here. If you want a new subdirectory to be created or use a new location you can adjust that here.

4. **Preview your blog locally**:
   ```bash
   quarto preview
   ```
   Your browser should open displaying localhost in the address bar and the default Quarto blog with sample posts.

#### Understanding Blog vs. Website Structure

The key architectural difference between a blog and a website is content organization:

**Website** (your academic site):
- Static pages at the root level (`index.qmd`, `about.qmd`, `cv.qmd`)
- Content rarely changes
- Navigation via navbar links

**Blog** (this project):
- A `posts/` directory containing individual posts
- Each post lives in its own subfolder: `posts/post-name/index.qmd`
- Homepage automatically generates a listing of posts
- Posts have metadata (date, author, categories) that enables automation

#### Configuring for GitHub Pages

Because this is a project site (not your user site), Quarto needs to know the base URL to generate correct links.

Be careful here. This is of "type" blog, but you will have a section "website."

1. **Edit `_quarto.yml`** to add the site URL and configure output:
   ```yaml
   project:
     type: website
	 site-url: https://your-website-url.example.com # you must change this appropriately for RSS feeds to work properly
     output-dir: docs

   website:
     site-url: "https://username.github.io/blog"
     title: "Your Blog Title"
     description: "A place for thinking out loud"
     right:
      - about.qmd
      - icon: github
        href: https://github.com/
		
   format:
     html:
       theme:
         - cosmo
         - brand
       css: styles.css	
   ```
   
   Replace `username` with your actual GitHub username. The `site-url` field ensures RSS feeds and internal links use the correct base path (`/blog`).

2. **Customize the about page** by editing `about.qmd`:
   ```yaml
   ---
   title: "About This Blog"
   ---

   [Explain what you plan to write about, why you're maintaining this blog, or what readers can expect]
   ```

#### Creating Blog Posts

You need to be careful now whether you are in your website repository or in your blog repository. Each is its own entity. 

Posts are just separate Quarto documents with structured metadata. The metadata isn't just decorative—it enables automatic listing pages, RSS feeds, and category filtering.

1. **Create a new post directory**:

	This command assumes you are alread in the base directory for you blog repository. 
	
   ```bash
   mkdir -p posts/first-post
   ```

2. **Create the post file** `posts/first-post/index.qmd`:
   Be careful about cutting and pasting. A missing set of hyphens or changes in white space can break the yaml structure. 
   
   ```yaml
   ---
   title: "My First Blog Post"
   author: "Your Name"
   date: "2024-01-15"
   categories: [thoughts, meta]
   ---

   ## Why I'm Starting This Blog

   [Your content here]

   This is a space for less polished thinking than my academic work requires. I plan to use it for...
   ```
   
   Before you start writing an essay just create a minimal entry and confirm that things are working before you proceed. 

3. **Preview the post**:
   on your localhost laptop
   
   ```bash
   quarto preview
   ```
   Navigate to your new post from the homepage listing.

The homepage (`index.qmd`) **automatically** generates a listing of all posts in the `posts/` directory, sorted by date. You don't need to manually maintain this list—Quarto reads the YAML metadata from each post.

#### Deployment

The deployment process is identical to your academic website:

1. **Build the site**:

   ```bash
   quarto render
   ```

2. **Commit and push**:

   ```bash
   git add .
   git commit -m "Initial blog setup"
   git push
   ```

3. **Configure GitHub Pages**: Navigate to repository Settings → Pages → Source: Deploy from branch → Branch: main → Folder: /docs → Save

Your blog will be available at `https://username.github.io/blog` within a few minutes.

#### Practice Exercises

For reference you can always consult the web page for blogs on the Quarto [website](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-blog.html).

Create three minimal blog posts with different metadata configurations to understand how Quarto uses this information:

1. **A post without categories**: Observe that it still appears in the listing but has no category tags.

2. **Two posts with overlapping categories**: Create posts tagged with `[research, methods]` and `[research, teaching]`. Notice how the category system creates implicit connections between posts.

3. **Posts with different dates**: Create posts dated a week apart. Verify that the listing page automatically orders them chronologically.

After creating each post, run `quarto preview` to see how the homepage listing updates automatically.

**Why the `/docs` output directory?** GitHub Pages expects site files in either the repository root or a `/docs` folder. Using `/docs` keeps your source files (`.qmd`) separate from generated HTML, making the repository more maintainable.

**Why `site-url` matters:** Without this field, Quarto assumes your site deploys at the domain root. For a project site at a subpath (`/blog`), links would break. The `site-url` tells Quarto to prepend `/blog` to all internal links and configure RSS feeds correctly.

**Directory structure philosophy:** Each post in its own folder allows you to keep related files (images, data files) co-located with the post content. This modular organization scales better than dumping everything in a single directory.
